title: Kebabs From Every Corner: A Michelin-Starred Chef Bets Phoenix Is Ready for Regional India
excerpt: Chef Sujan Sarkar's NADU brings a coast-to-coast kebab program to the desert, wagering that American diners are hungry for an India beyond butter chicken.
body:
For decades, the American idea of Indian food has been a short list: butter chicken, naan, samosas, a lunch buffet with a steam tray of saag paneer. NADU, the Michelin-recognized concept from Chicago chef Sujan Sarkar, is opening in Phoenix this summer with a deliberate argument against that narrowing — and it is making the case one kebab at a time.

## A menu built like a map

NADU, which means "homeland," opened its first location in Chicago to critical acclaim, where its specialty was regional curries drawn from across the subcontinent. The Phoenix outpost, at Desert Ridge Marketplace, takes a different tack. According to Pujan Sarkar — the chef's brother and longtime mentee, who is steering the new kitchen — the restaurant is anchored by a regional kebab program that reads like a tour of India.

The lineup includes Galouti Kebab from Lucknow, the melt-in-the-mouth minced-meat specialty born in the kitchens of the Nawabs; Bhatti Ka Murgh from Punjab; and a Chapli Kebab from the northwest frontier. Rounding it out are a Duck Seekh Kebab, Stuffed Paneer Tikka, Goli Kebab and a signature Bihari Kebab. Each carries the fingerprint of a specific place — a quiet rebuttal to the flattening of "Indian food" into a single house style.

"Most popular Indian restaurants in the U.S. serve primarily cuisine from the north and south of India," Pujan told The Arizona Republic, framing NADU's wider regional sweep as the whole point. The kebab program, he said, is meant to "help guests understand that Indian food can be different from what they're used to."

## Context and background

NADU arrives inside a larger reordering of Indian dining in America. Sujan Sarkar's flagship Indienne earned a Michelin star in Chicago and has since expanded to New York's Hudson Yards. His company has been opening at pace — Ayra in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, a second Indienne, and now a second NADU. Phoenix itself has become an unlikely hotspot: Indibar by Masti Hospitality opened there in 2025 and is adding a 10-course tasting room called Lehr this fall.

The momentum is not isolated. Restaurant industry researchers note that 52% of American consumers say they have tried Indian food and liked it, and upscale Indian rooms are now operating in New York, Chicago, San Francisco and Los Angeles. The cuisine is finally being treated as worthy of the fine-dining and chef-driven treatment long extended to French, Japanese and Italian food.

## Diaspora impact

For Indian Americans, a restaurant like NADU does something a buffet never could: it sees them. A second-generation kid from a Bihari family can find a Bihari kebab on a Phoenix menu; a Lucknow grandmother's galouti gets plated with intention rather than apology. That specificity is its own form of recognition — proof that the diaspora's regional identities are legible, valuable and worth charging fine-dining prices for.

It also reshapes the conversation NRIs have with their non-Indian friends and colleagues. When the menu insists that a Punjabi bhatti chicken and a frontier chapli kebab are not interchangeable, it teaches American diners to hold India's diversity in their heads — the way they already do for Italy's regions or Mexico's. The cocktail program leans the same direction, building drinks around turmeric, saffron, chili, ginger and curry leaf rather than treating Indian flavor as a garnish.

## What's next

NADU was expected to open at Desert Ridge Marketplace in late June, with July reservations available on OpenTable and dinner service running Tuesday through Sunday. If the kebab-forward, region-hopping format draws crowds in Phoenix — a market already proving its appetite for ambitious Indian food — expect the template to travel. The broader question NADU is testing is whether American diners will keep rewarding restaurants that refuse to simplify. For a generation of NRIs who grew up explaining that their home food was never just "curry," the answer cannot come fast enough.

Sources: The Arizona Republic (azcentral.com); Restaurant Business Online; Technomic/Datassential consumer research.
